items.bodyEn: Yokkaichi means 'fourth-day market.' In medieval Japan periodic markets opened on fixed days of the lunar month, here the 4th, 14th and 24th, and towns grew around them. The name is recorded from the fifteenth century. Place names across Japan keep the old calendar: 三日市, 五日市, 八日市, 十日市. 市 now means 'city,' but it began as the market square.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten / 角川日本地名大辞典, entry 四日市: 四の日に立つ定期市から

items.bodyEn: Hiroshige's Yokkaichi print shows no inns, only weather. On the bank of the Mie River a traveler sprints after his hat as the wind snatches it away, another crosses a plank bridge with his rain cape flapping, and the willows stream sideways. The riverside path is the Tōkaidō itself. Few images of Edo travel are this funny and this true.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Tōkaidō gojūsan-tsugi (Hōeidō ed., 1833–34), 'Yokkaichi: Mie River'

items.titleEn: Fork in the Road to Ise
items.bodyEn: Just south of Yokkaichi the Tōkaidō forked at Hinaga no Oiwake. The left branch ran to Ise, and a torii raised there in 1774 told pilgrims they had stepped onto the shrine's road. Yokkaichi itself was a port on Ise Bay with 98 inns in 1843, and later the home of Banko ware pottery.
items.ja: {日永|ひなが}の{追分|おいわけ}
items.sourceNote: 東海道宿村大概帳 (1843): Yokkaichi 98 hatago; Hinaga no Oiwake torii (安永3, 1774)

items.bodyEn: 〜ものの concedes a fact and then reports that it did not lead where you expected: 買ったものの、一度も着ていない, I bought it, but have never worn it. It belongs to writing and careful speech, and its second half states what happened, never a request or a plan. 〜とはいえ, 'that said,' is freer and can open a sentence.
items.ja: {買|か}ったものの、{一度|いちど}も{着|き}ていない
items.kana: かったものの、いちどもきていない
